Messages.Author: lk...@pop.mpls.uswest.net
Messages.Body:
I've been playing Jyhad since about an hour after it hit the shelves.
I've been on the Web for less than 6 months. I was kinda pleased to
stumble on to this group, and commented on a couple decks. happened to
mention a 4 card limit. Apparently you guys have been hashing this out
for some time. Well while you guys were arguing I was playing cards.

Quite frankly I don't see how you get any pleasure from playing the same
6 to 10 cards over and over and over. Friends come over sit down and by
the time your first vampire hits the table everybody knows your whole
deck all your strengths and weaknesses. Then everybody takes all of five
minutes to size up the table. Then spend the next 2 to 4 hours and only
play six cards. How Sad

The Reason we started the JCL in the first place was to curb the Malk's
and anyone who says the malk's dominate a 4CL game should come play with
me some time.

The strength of my decks is their versatility and in a large game of
Jyhad versatility will quite frankly save your ass as you move from prey
to prey. Allowing yourself to adjust your deck on the fly to have
something that can get past anything your prey might throw at you. And
react to a new predator for that matter.

I even heard 4CL decks are unreliable. If that's the case you need to
work on your deck building skills. I'm sorry if I pissed you all off. I
thought only 8 people even knew about this game last week
And it appears you guys only play with 6 card decks. It's really kinda
sad.

Messages.Author: Andy Kaiser
Messages.Body:
I noticed this too, and was kind of surprised - people don't usually jump
all over each other like that around here. While I don't agree with 4 card
limits (too much like the dreaded Magic), the folks that I play with use a
house rule of a 10% limit. (For example, you've got a 90 card deck, you
can have 9 of a particular card.) The reason 4CL's work in Magic, but not
in V:TES is simply because, on the average, V:TES decks seem to run about
twice as large as Magic decks. If you have a limit of 4 cards, you may
never get the cards you need. (To illustrate this, try playing a 90 card
deck in a Magic Tourney...)

At any rate, I agree with you that decks made up of 40 Wakes, etc. are
extremely boring, not to mention darn annoying. You ought to try that 10%
idea, though - it keeps the spirit of variety alive, while not limiting
decks.

Andy

4CL decks *are* unreliable, compared to their no-limit cousins. If you
can only put 4 copies of a particular card into your deck, you are less
likely to draw it than if you can put in 8 or 10, and if there are
no good substitutes for the card you want to use, your deck will be
less reliable because of it.

Your characterization of our decks as having only six different cards
in them is pretty inaccurate, I think. I've recently been playing a
deck that's based on small vampires with celerity, mostly Brujah, and
a bunch of allies, and guns. I'm using 10 Arms Dealers, and I'd like
to have more. If I were playing under a 4CL, I wouldn't be allowed to
use so many Arms Dealers; yet they're the most useful ally for this
deck because they don't cost any pool, and they can even go find the
guns for me if I'm not drawing them.

Another deck I'm playing is a serious bloodgain deck using mostly large
Ventrue, with 7 Minion Tap and about 8 Fifth Tradition. Minion Tap/5th
Trad isn't reliable when you can only have 4 of each of them.

Most importantly, 4 card limits don't stop abusive combos from happening.
They just make them happen less often.

Have you noticed that most decks built under a 4CL have exactly 4
copies of every card they consider most useful? Doesn't this indicate
that the 4CL isn't 'encouraging creative deckbuilding' but merely
forcing people to use inferior cards when they're not allowed to use
the good ones anymore? Wouldn't it encourage creativity even more
to simply ban all the relatively powerful cards?

Josh

Erm, no. This is not quite what the argument over 4CL/NCL has to be
about (of course, it can be about it).

Let's just say that you want to play a Setite Corruption deck. It isn't
necessarily going to be the best or most effective of decks but it's
what you want to play. If 4CL is in place, you can't do it effectively
because you can only use 4 of them. Now, in a NL environment, you could
maybe put something up to 20 of them in which might be about right.
Then you could have assorted masters, assorted modifiers, a few actions,
maybe a vote or two, a bit of equipment. The thing is, NCL isn't about
cutting down the number of different cards you have in your deck - it's
about allowing you to have as many cards as you need of each type in a
deck.

If you look at many of the decks on the group or on the Not the Jyhad
Deck Archive, you'll often see that they require a large number of one
or two cards but then they diversify off into lots of other little cards
which only have one or two of each in the deck to provide back up. I
mean, in almost every deck I play I have Sudden Reversals, Blood Dolls,
maybe an STI or two, a few of each of the skills I'm using (I tend to
use odd combos for a bit of fun but which means most vamps don't have
both at superior), maybe a bit of stealth, a bit of equipment possibly,
a few vote cards (even if it's something like Surprise Influence). And
then, if I was playing a heavy stealth deck (for instance) I would use
lots of different stealth cards to give me the flexibility to tap out
your vamps (Faceless Night), that maneuver I need (Swallowed), that
extra stealth from my other vamps (Cloak) etc. etc.

Here's some of the key points on this I've heard to date, in no
particular order, and in no particualr response to any particular
point you've tried to make;

1. Most strategies which people try to control in Jyhad with a card
limit have access to simple variants of card names, and thus avoid
limitation (Malk sneak 'n bleed, and vote decks, primarily). Decks
which rely on a particular few cards (usually rush combat) have a more
difficult time under card limits.

2. Esoteric deck construction, a long standing hobby for many, is
completely devalued under CL. Oddball clans are used even less.
Setite Corruption, Ravnos SenseDep, some Assamite concepts, are not
just difficult, but impossible to do. As such, more outlandish deck
concepts aren't explored as often.

3. If you only want four of each card, you're more than free to do so
under NCL...

4. Jyhad doesn't "ratio up" the way M:t$ does... Having a higher
amount of a particular card hardly guarantees a win, it just means you
have to find a way to play it more often. (this stems from the higher
card flow rate in Jyhad, and the fact that each individual card has
less impact on the ultimate outcome of the game...)

5. Card limits don't do much to fix "broken" combos, they simply don't
happen as often. This was true of M:t$ as well; the real stability of
the game came from the introduction of the concept of Type II, and the
phasing out of overpowered cards by retirement of expansions. By
then, though, everyone was so used to the 4CL, there was little reason
to switch. Officially, there's no card limit to the basic rules of
M:t$, either... That's a tournament thing.

More to follow if I think of them...

Messages.Author: Jaysen Knight
Messages.Body:
A few points from a NCL believer.

What I can appreciate about card limits:

1. CL means fewer cards to collect. I AM SUITCASE BOY....
which can really suck. Do you know how hard it is to get 6/8
Tombs and 6/8 RTI's without being willing to trade my other
rares? I just can't trade a bunch of cards to make sure I
can create my new 'killer deck', and then a couple of months
later, trade those cards for my new killer deck. I am a sick
sick boy....I need help. No...I will not give all of my
cards away just to alleviate my sickness:)

2. CL encourages different combos to try to get the same
result. You get an appreciation for some wallpaper cards
with CL that you don't necessarily use with NCL. Is this
truly a good thing? Not sure of that, but I could see where
a NCL player could learn a few 'tricks' playing CL. One
of those "Hmmmm, I didn't think of that" kind of things.
It won't happen often to a good player, but it could.

I remember reading a post on this group about a year ago,
regarding a tournament in Europe - 1 card limit. Wow.
I don't even know what to think about that, but it would
be interesting to see.

3. If most have 200-300 cards to make their decks, and the
local card bully has waaaayyy more, then CL may level the
playing field a little. My arguement is not to play with
a card bully, buttt sometimes you do what you have to do.

I'm running out of stuff that I can appreciate here....yup,
I'm about done with that. However....VTES is a NCL game,
some of the things I love about NCL.

1. Variety in deck types. Only in NCL would you see ET's
'Everyone Dies Deck'. Using many, many Caitiff's to play
many Anarch Revolts and a Smiling Jack as needed to kill
every Meth at the table - with you being last. (It was
posted to The Corruptor's site if you want to look at it).
You would never see this deck, or most others, in CL - it
simply would not be effective. Which brings me to point
#2....

2. Effectiveness. Why is S&B so effective? It only
requires two components (S&B) and so requires fewer cards
to pull off the combo. A rush deck, by comparison, requires
many more cards to get going, to whit:
1. An action (or master) card to get into combat.
2. Combat cards to stay in combat (a combat deck can
be foiled by many different methods - Elysium, Mariel, a
simple dodge or maneuver) by limiting movement, restarting
combat after S:CE, etc. This can take several cards on
occasion.
Note, a Mariel in a secure haven can destroy all but the
most robust Rush Combat decks - something CL cannot give you.
3. Combat cards to cause damage. After you have got
into combat, and stayed in combat, you have to hurt the vamp
you attack. This takes more cards.

To summarize. A S&B deck requires a simple combo of two
types of cards. A good Rush Combat deck (like many) requires
more types of cards to be successful. VTES is a game of
combos, the harder the combo is to pull off - the less
effective the deck (even when the rarer combo has great
results when it does work). CL makes multi-card combos very
hard to pull off.

There are so many more arguements as to why CL kills so many
decks (the discipline arguement come to mind), but that is for
another day. I have said too much already. No, really, I
have.

Nope. Though it is true that playing said combos can allow you to do

sit there and slow the game so that HE can decide what happens. He's

just Wake normally) and then pummel you with Celerity and guns (it was
Toreador) but can also pull your votes down in the mean time. He's also
done a very nice Gangrel one where you just basically sit there and
build up one very cool vampire supplemented by one or two others who can
untap and stop any action. He could basically have drawn the game out
for as long as he wanted whilst others depleted their pools trying to
oust him. The only reason the game was a little shorter was because,
unfortunately, the DCI rules do mean that you have to finish a game
after a set time period (normally, 2 hours). In a normal game played
amongst friends, his deck could easily have been the 5 hour affair you
wanted. Lots of talking, diplomacy, jibes etc. as people tried to take
out Raven/Camille, lots of opportunity for fun.

>I prefer a long game with my freinds a 5 hour affair with
>plenty of beer and conversation.I'm not trying to get in 5 short games just
>to rack up a few EASY victory points.

NCL doesn't force you to play the game like that. Clever deck
construction and design can force the game to slow down. You just need
to know what you're doing. And, no offense, a stalwart 4CL player isn't
likely to be able to construct a deck under NCL to do that, simply due
to the lack of experience (of course, that goes the other way round).

> Another reason a lot of people play
>NCL is because it is easier to play. They rely on thier cards more than

>thier skill in playing them.

Not necessarily. Just because I have 8 Taste of Vitaes in a deck
instead of 4 doesn't mean I necessarily play them more effectively etc.

And part of the emphasis of NCL is that of deck design. The generalised
argument here is as follows. Let's say I choose to create an intercept
deck, from Auspex. Under 4CL, I might want to say have 5 different
Auspex cards with 4 cards each. Maybe a few more, whatever. The thing
is, part of the special-ness, the individuality of each card is lost
because you look at The Spirit's Touch and Precognition and think "Hey,
cool, here are two different cards which give me +1 intercept. I'll
have to have both of these." The same would go for cards to get you
reliably into combat, reliably get stealth, reliably prevent damage,
reliably bleed etc. Okay, now, if I get into the same situation where
I'm deciding to put intercept cards into a deck, I'm put in the position
of deciding what's more important for me in the deck. Should I try and
use The Spirit's Touch to try and get the maneuver so that I can get
away from the people I block and hit them at range? Should I use
Precognition so that I can stay at close range, prevent their hand
strike and hit them back? But what happens if they hit me with a BIG
hand strike and I can't prevent it all? And what happens if that isn't
enough intercept? Should I throw some Enhanced Senses in just in case?
But then that stops my ability to defend myself in combat....... And if
someone tries to hit me with a cross-table vote.... maybe I should try
and drop a couple of Eagle's Sight in there, just in case.....

That's another aspect of skill which comes into NCL more than 4CL. In
NCL, you have to consider the impact of any given card from all points
of view. I want to do presence based bleed... what's going to be better
for me? Social Charm, Enchant Kindred or Legal Manipulations. Each is
distinct - Legal Manipulations has the blood cost... does my deck have
the blood gain for it....

>in short a NCL game focuses on the cards while a
>4CL game focues on the players.

The standard argument here is that you have five real cards for it:

1) Bum's Rush
2) Ambush
3) Haven Uncovered
4) Archon
5) Bloodhunt/War Party

I put number 5 as one because you're unlikely to be able to play both in
the same deck. Bum's Rush is Bloodhunt and Haven Uncovered are quite
similar in that they act like a kind of semi-permanent. The thing is,
any rush deck with teeth will be able to take out a vampire in one or
two combats hopefully. None of the last three provide any maneuvers for
your vamps (I don't think Archon does) and one of the nice points about
Bum's Rush and Ambush is that they have that nice maneuver which can
encourage people to block the action (allowing nasty surprises with
Hidden Lurker). In a heavy rush deck, your master phases may well be
taken up with a few blood gain cards (The Rack (also encourages people
to steal it so you can (D) it back and hope they block) and hunting
grounds) and maybe a few long term pool gain cards since these take up
few master card slots in your deck but can use the master phase slots in
the game. Playing only one Haven Uncovered per turn really limits you
and having to purchase a Parthenon makes it more expensive for you as
well and leaves you less pool for vamps. You can't use 4 or 5 if you
can't pass the votes easily so in a standard rush deck, only the first
three are viable. Ambush won't work if the vampires tapped and if
you're having to ensure vampires are tapped (Anarch Troublemaker, say)
then that takes other cards from your deck. Of course, some decks
thrive with Ambush but what's the point of using other cards in your
deck to tap out your prey's vampires when you're only going to be using
it for four cards? And things like Anarch Troublemakers take away from
playing your Haven Uncovered's, and if you're taking actions such as
Mind Numb or Jar the Soul (as you could do in a Giovanni deck), well,
that's your Bum's Rush/Ambush actions made more difficult, isn't it?

4-knights opening? You think that's your best move? Ever try a King's
Knight's Pawn opening? Surprises the hell out of your opponent and actually
puts you in a good tactical position. The Danish Gambit puts you behind two
pawns, but while your opponent spends all of his first few moves with a single
pawn, you have developed half of your pieces. And the English Opening, while
I have never mastered it, is loved by many, and countered by few. I suppose
if you're playing against Grand Masters, you may want to stick to the
tried-and-true methods, but the fact is, chess evolves. New strategies have
been coming around since the game was conceived. And your best bet depends as
much on your opponent's mindset as on the actual pieces and moves. If your
opponents are all set on using the 4 Knights Opening, you should exploit that.
Do something that will prevent them from moving their Knights. Cut off from
what they want to do will leave them frustrated and open for the easy kill.

> Now we play with a 4-move-look-ahead-limit. It's much more fun. We find
ourselves making
> moves we never would have made before. It's fun to try to win making only a
few great

(or worse)
> moves you made earlier due to 4MLAL.
>
> Plus, it's less intimidating to newbies, who can't look that far ahead
anyhow.
>

Yes, but if you only look 4 moves ahead, you miss out on a lot of interesting
strategies. The English Opening and Danish Gambit seem stupid. Castling will
always occur. You will almost never pull off a Knight fork. Once you get
down to a King and a Queen vs. a King, whether or not you win will be based
entirely on luck, since it usually takes more than 4 moves to finish them off,
and stalemate is still possible. You will never know the sheer joy of having
2 fianchetto'ed Bishops. In NL, you can do all these things. Sure, maybe
4MLAL will be good for the beginners, but once you've advanced beyond that
stage, why pollute the game?

If you cannot see my references to Jyhad above, look closer. I think I've
finished making my point.

Also... how the hell do you limit look-ahead in chess?!? I could see limiting
it on a computer, but at certain times you just *know* that a Knight in a
certain position is good because it can do something in 5 more moves. And
stuff like that.

Well, also Ascendance costs 1 master phase per pool gained, whereas Short Term

Come now, let's not be naive. Is it more likely that you will own 12 Torn
Signposts, or that you will own 4 each of Increased Strength, Fists of Death,
and Fire in the Blood? The fact is, in 4CL, multiples of rares are needed to
make up for the fact that you are limited to 4 of each common. Give arguments
of increased variability if you will, but don't try to tell me that 4CL is
more fair to those with limited cards. It is much easier to buy (or get
someone to give you) 12 of any commons you need than it is to get 4 of each of
the broken rares you need in a 4CL deck. Many good NL decks can be made with
only commons and a few uncommons. The same cannot be said for 4CL. And with
Immortal Grapple now uncommon in Sabbat, this is even more so. Sure, there
were a few mistakes with rares being too powerful, but this is only augmented
by placing an artificial limit on the number of each common you can use.

ber...@cco.caltech.edu wrote:

> But the game should be based mostly on your deck construction and playing

I do not believe that NCL demands higher deck construction or playing
skill. The examples you give are perfectly reasonable, but in a 4CL
group you see many unusual situations, and I think this gives you a
better understanding of game possibilities. I'm trying very hard to be
reasonable about this, so I'll add that NCL gives better insight into
the building of "competitive" decks. These are just different aspects of
game skill, which are not incompatible.

>
> Further, I find that the "luck" in a 4CL deck *isn't* whether or not you get
> bleed cards when you need them, but it's whether you get the GtU or Scouting
> Mission when you really need 3 blood on your vampire. In a good NL deck,

> you'll *know* whether GtU or Scouting Mission is better to use more of.
>

IMHO predictability is not the only goal in jyhad. Besides, deciding
wether to keep a card in hand or not (like a disguised weapon, when you
hope an useful weapon will come soon) is an interesting tactical
problem, and it makes Elder Library, Cassandra & such fairly rewarding.

>
> The point is, most of us *have* tried 4CL before learning the errors of our
> ways.

This is true. Most NCL players have tried 4CL. And most 4CL players
have tried 4CL. So what? I've read in several posts that European
players _tend_ to play 4CL, unlike their lucky American buddies. (lucky,
because of card prices & availability!) What does that mean? I don't
know.

> When my friend first put 11 Taste of Vitae in a deck, we howled "4 of a
> kind." But then we realized... "Hey! Now you can actually build an effective
> Tremere deck. And without huge multiples of the rares." When the Nos player
> first used 6 Faceless Night, we screamed, "use Elder Impersonation." But we
> soon realized the joys of subtle variations. Now there is more strategy to
> deck-building than simple choosing a clan and piling on 4 of the useful cards
> in each discipline. And when I used 6 Ascendance in lieu of Short Terms and

> Protracted Investment, I was laughed at. But we realized the tradeoff of

> cards for speed. More cards can give you a quicker combo sometimes, but the
> number of cards itself is the cost. Soon we realized that there was more to
> the game than bleed, block, stealth, intercept, fight. A vote deck popped up
> that was actually usable. It was never viable before because of a lack of

> protection in combat. The Giovanni made an appearance. And the Nos became a

> real annoyance, rather than a speed bump.

The only things I can say are:
- I've seen and played many, many effective 4CL Tremere decks, (what
rares are that important to this deck, please?)
- Choosing a clan and piling on 4 of the useful cards in each
discipline is a very bad way to design a 4CL deck. It won't get you
anywhere. That's why I said that deck building skills are important to
4CL players (as to NCL). A deck you design like that is very likely to
get toasted easily at any average 4CL game.

>
> If I could better express the degree to which my playgroup was improved by NL,
> I would, but I suspect I am talking to a small cadre of zealots out there.
> I've said myself that if you're in the majority, there's a good chance you're
> wrong, but in this case I stand by my convictions.

I'm sure this is true. Your playgroup was such that NCL was a better
thing. You all feel it was a good decision. My group feels exactly the
same about 4CL. I never tried to convert anybody. I just think it
strange how some people feel it's important that I see how NCL is so
much better.

> House rules aside, the
> game was designed for NL, and that's how it should be played.

This argument sounds lame to me. If I feel 4CL is better, and the
creator of the game tells me NCL is the way it should be, how should
this convince me? It could incite me to try NCL and find out by myself.
Sure, I've done that. But, please, Mr WotC and WW and LBJ, don't feel
upset if I do it my way. I still love you all :)

> In your own
> group, however, feel free to place whatever limits you want. I suggest a 0
> card limit myself. Or maybe a 4 card minimum (at least 4 copies of each
> card). Or how about requiring a deck to be constructed of 80 copies of a
> single card. If you don't own enough of any card, you can't play. I'll play
> a Restoration deck, myself. 8)

I'll play a Renagade Deck myself. Have a nice day!

I disagree completely. One of the reasons Jyhad (4CL or NCL) is great
is that you can build massively successful decks with only 10 or 12
uncommons or rares. But, as I've said over and over again (with NO
answer from anybody, sadly), being successful isn't all there is in a
game of Jyhad. I play to win (partly), but also tohave fun. So putting 4
of each broken card is definitely bad IMHO.

>

> And it is also the only one that can be made with mostly commons.

Yes, in 4CL S&B is the champ. So what? It only matters if everybody
keeps on playing them, which is unlikely since after a while you'd get
bored. And (see above), I believe it is absolutely false that S&B is the
only competitive 4CL deck made up of commons.

Actually yes. Someone always plays S&B until shamed out of it. Since this
shame out of "cheesy decks" is subjective, you may be able to have a Lasombra
S&B or a Malkavian Disguised Weapon deck, but not a Malkavian S&B. But it
only takes a small bit of deviation before someone decides that the Malk DW
deck is really an S&B. So, I always, always, always hear people on the
newsgroup talking about how they need to shame people out of playing S&B.
This resort to metagaming (a dirty word in Live Action Role-Playing, but not
quite so bad in Jyhad) to even things out.

Also, in my playgroup back home, we had an S&B deck that was consistently
played and was consistently ganged-up on. This was before we switched to NL.
He whined about being ganged up on, but he still always won.
